reconciliation.source: Stanford Review PDF page 30 (slide 3-30), contrasted with page 29
reconciliation.finding: Page 29 defines an unsigned arccos angle; page 30 also lists -pi/2 for orthogonality.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: For nonzero real vectors define theta in [0,pi]; orthogonality gives theta=pi/2. The zero vector is algebraically orthogonal to every vector but has no direction or angle.

reconciliation.finding: The word component denotes a signed scalar, not a vector.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: For b nonzero, signed component is (x dot b)/norm(b); projection vector is ((x dot b)/(b dot b))b; projection length is abs(x dot b)/norm(b). If b is unit, the formulas simplify but the scalar/vector distinction remains. Reversing b changes the signed component, not the projection onto span(b).

reconciliation.finding: Basic Gram-Schmidt assumes independent input. Generalized Gram-Schmidt explicitly skips a zero residual instead of normalizing it.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: Maintain span of accepted vectors equal to the span of processed inputs. Normalize only a nonzero residual. A zero residual means the current vector lies in the previous span, including a zero first input. In finite precision, exact zero and a chosen numerical tolerance are different decisions.

reconciliation.source: Stanford Review PDF pages 26-31 and Stanford QR PDF pages 2-7
reconciliation.finding: These selected Stanford pages treat real vectors and transpose, not complex Hermitian geometry.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: Use x* y for the chapter's complex convention, conjugate-linear in the first slot. Euclidean norm is sqrt(sum abs(x_i)^2). Orthogonal projection onto span(b) is b(b* x)/(b* b). Do not use x^T x as a complex squared norm; x=(1,i) has x^T x=0 and x* x=2. This complex extension is independently derived and reconciled with Oxford, not falsely attributed to these real-only pages.

reconciliation.finding: The selected pages do not define general induced matrix norms. Stanford Review page 26 gives the Euclidean vector norm and its axioms.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: If a question uses ||A||_2, explicitly define the induced/operator norm sup_{x!=0} ||Ax||_2/||x||_2, rather than silently confusing it with Frobenius norm. Supply an independent proof or a separately reviewed written source for any advanced operator-norm result. Do not credit a matrix-norm theory to these selected notes.

reconciliation.finding: The source's dimension-infinity parenthesis says no basis, in a finite-dimensional review context.
reconciliation.chapter_rule: Keep this chapter finite-dimensional, or say no finite basis when discussing infinite dimension. The zero space has the empty basis and dimension zero. Do not claim that every infinite-dimensional space lacks a basis.

reconciliation.finding: The fresh PDF text and visually inspected pages explicitly use nonnegativity with equality if and only if the vector is zero. Those source statements are correct. Remove the prior audit's claim of positivity slips; strict positivity for nonzero vectors is an equivalent instructional restatement.
For x+2y+z=0, the stated second basis vector (0,2,-1) is outside the plane. Use (0,1,-2); (x,y,-x-2y)=x(1,0,-1)+y(0,1,-2).

The stated assumption m!=n for arbitrary signed integers does not rule out m=-n. Cosine frequencies m and -m define the same function, so orthogonality requires distinct absolute frequencies; handle zero separately. For nonzero frequency, squared norm is pi; constant 1 has squared norm 2pi. The sine/cosine odd-integrand identity remains valid for all integer frequencies.

Oxford uses sum z_i conjugate(w_i), linear in first argument. The chapter convention sum conjugate(z_i) w_i is conjugate-linear in first and linear in second. Thus p_b(x)=b <b,x>/<b,b>; the Oxford-convention equivalent uses <x,b>/<b,b>. Do not transpose these numerators blindly.

The source gives integral x^3(x^2-1/3) from -1 to 1 as 2/7 and a nonzero projection. The integrand x^5-x^3/3 is odd, so the integral and projection of x^3 onto span(1,x^2) are zero. The orthogonal polynomial x^2-1/3 and squared norm 8/45 are correct. Residual squared norm is integral x^6=2/7.
